"Below are questions proposed for a research problem, each with the reframing behind it. Classify each one.
kind: \"reframe\" if it changes what is computed, measured or ordered so that more compute buys something it did not before; \"copies\" if it only runs the same computation more times, on more items, or side by side; \"other\" otherwise.
meets_criterion: \"yes\" or \"no\" for this criterion: It removes a step-after-step dependency that one answer waits on (time steps, chain iterations or solver iterations), so that those steps are computed at the same time. Running independent copies side by side, or splitting each single step across GPUs, does not count.
Give for each a quote from the proposal and a reason of at most 25 words. Decide only from the text below; do not use tools.
Problem:
Bayesian calibration of rainfall-runoff models for river catchments, which needs long MCMC chains.
Proposals: [{\"index\":1,\"title\":\"Batched time-step rainfall-runoff simulation on GPUs for ensemble likelihood evaluation\",\"field\":\"Computational hydrology and rainfall-runoff model calibration\",\"sequential_part\":\"Within one parameter proposal, the watershed state must be updated recursively through daily time steps; each state depends on the previous day.\",\"restructure\":\"Keep the daily recurrence exactly but vectorize the state update over thousands of parameter sets or catchments on a GPU, so the sequential time loop becomes a short sequence of wide parallel kernels.\",\"condition\":\"Concurrent parameter sets number in the hundreds to thousands so the per-step update saturates GPU throughput, and CPU-GPU transfer cost is amortized across many likelihood evaluations.\",\"baselines\":\"Single-thread CPU and OpenMP multi-core runs of the same solver; compare wall-clock time and numerical agreement of streamflow and objective values within a set tolerance.\",\"first_test\":\"Benchmark one model with 1024 parameter sets over 30 years of daily forcing data on CPU vs GPU; roughly 30-60 minutes of GPU time.\"},{\"index\":2,\"title\":\"Many short independent MCMC chains with rank-normalized early stopping\",\"field\":\"Bayesian inference for hydrological model calibration\",\"sequential_part\":\"A single MCMC chain is inherently sequential; every sample waits on the previous accepted sample, so long chains cannot be shortened naively.\",\"restructure\":\"Replace one long chain with hundreds of independent chains launched together on a GPU, using vectorized log-likelihood calls, then pool draws after burn-in and monitor rank-normalized R-hat and effective sample size.\",\"condition\":\"The posterior basin supports mixing across seeds, proposal scales can be tuned or adapted, and GPU memory is sufficient for many chains; isolated modes are handled with multiple seeds or tempering if present.\",\"baselines\":\"A single long CPU chain with equal total iterations; compare R-hat, ESS per GPU-second, posterior parameter summaries, and predictive streamflow uncertainty intervals.\",\"first_test\":\"Run 200 chains for 5000 iterations on a small existing rainfall-runoff posterior; roughly 1-2 GPU-hours.\"},{\"index\":3,\"title\":\"Speculative multi-branch proposal evaluation for sequential-hazard MCMC\",\"field\":\"Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithms applied to Bayesian calibration\",\"sequential_part\":\"The accept/reject decision at step t determines the starting point for step t+1, so the chain cannot evaluate the next proposal until the current decision is made.\",\"restructure\":\"At each step evaluate k candidate proposals from the current state in parallel on the GPU, then combine them via a statistically valid multi-proposal Metropolis-Hastings update, or use branch-and-rollback prefetching to reuse speculative evaluations.\",\"condition\":\"Log-likelihood evaluation dominates the runtime, and the acceptance rate and proposal diversity are high enough that parallel branches are useful for the chosen kernel.\",\"baselines\":\"Single-proposal Metropolis-Hastings with the same rainfall-runoff likelihood; compare effective sample size per GPU-second and posterior summary accuracy, and report wasted speculative evaluations.\",\"first_test\":\"Test the multi-proposal kernel on a cheap analytic proxy for the hydrologic posterior plus one batched likelihood run; measure candidates per accepted draw; roughly 1 GPU-hour.\"},{\"index\":4,\"title\":\"Neural likelihood emulator for accelerating rainfall-runoff calibration\",\"field\":\"Scientific machine learning for hydrological model calibration\",\"sequential_part\":\"Every MCMC likelihood call requires a multi-year rainfall-runoff simulation with sequential daily recurrence, and a long chain needs millions of such calls.\",\"restructure\":\"Build a GPU neural surrogate mapping parameters to likelihood values or summary signatures from offline simulator runs; evaluate the surrogate in large batches during MCMC, with periodic exact simulator re-evaluation to correct or diagnose drift.\",\"condition\":\"The surrogate is accurate inside the high-posterior region, its error is small relative to posterior width, and offline training runs cover the relevant prior or exploratory posterior region.\",\"baselines\":\"Exact simulator MCMC runs; compare posterior means, covariances, predictive intervals, and wall-clock time, and explicitly measure emulator-induced posterior shift.\",\"first_test\":\"Generate 10,000 offline simulator runs for one catchment, train a small MLP or Gaussian process, and measure validation error and prediction speedup; roughly 2-4 GPU-hours including data generation.\"},{\"index\":5,\"title\":\"Differentiable gradient-based HMC on GPUs to shorten sequential chains\",\"field\":\"Differentiable Bayesian inference for rainfall-runoff models\",\"sequential_part\":\"Random-walk Metropolis chains need very long sequential mixing because proposal directions are inefficient in high-dimensional parameter space.\",\"restructure\":\"Rewrite the rainfall-runoff recurrence in a differentiable framework and reverse-mode autodifferentiate the log-likelihood; run HMC or NUTS on GPU with multiple leapfrog trajectories in parallel, taking fewer sequential steps to reach the same effective sample size.\",\"condition\":\"The model and log-likelihood are differentiable with stable gradients, threshold or staircase terms can be smoothed, and GPU memory holds several leapfrog trajectories at once.\",\"baselines\":\"Existing random-walk Metropolis or DE-MC chains on CPU; compare effective sample size per second, posterior summary accuracy, and leapfrog energy diagnostics.\",\"first_test\":\"Implement a differentiable single-catchment model, check gradients with finite differences, and benchmark 100 warm-up HMC trajectories; roughly 1 GPU-hour.\"}]

Return only one JSON value, with no other text, that matches this JSON Schema:
{\"type\":\"object\",\"required\":[\"items\"],\"properties\":{\"items\":{\"type\":\"array\",\"items\":{\"type\":\"object\",\"required\":[\"index\",\"kind\",\"meets_criterion\",\"quote\",\"reason\"],\"properties\":{\"index\":{\"type\":\"integer\"},\"kind\":{\"type\":\"string\",\"enum\":[\"reframe\",\"copies\",\"other\"]},\"meets_criterion\":{\"type\":\"string\",\"enum\":[\"yes\",\"no\",\"NA\"]},\"quote\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"reason\":{\"type\":\"string\"}}}}}}"

Let me analyze each proposal against the criteria.

Criterion: "It removes a step-after-step dependency that one answer waits on (time steps, chain iterations or solver iterations), so that those steps are computed at the same time. Running independent copies side by side, or splitting each single step across GPUs, does not count."

Kind: "reframe" if it changes what is computed, measured or ordered so that more compute buys something it did not before; "copies" if it only runs the same computation more times, on more items, or side by side; "other" otherwise.

Proposal 1: Batched time-step simulation. The daily recurrence is kept exactly sequential; it just vectorizes over parameter sets. So the sequential time-step dependency remains — it's running the same computation on more items (parameter sets) side by side. This is "copies". Meets criterion: no, because the time-step dependency is not removed; independent parameter sets run side by side.

Proposal 2: Many short independent MCMC chains. Replaces one long chain with hundreds of independent chains. This is running independent copies side by side — "copies". Meets criterion: no, because independent chains running side by side doesn't count. However, one might argue that replacing a long chain with many short chains changes what is computed... Actually the sequential dependency within each chain remains; it's just parallel copies. The criterion explicitly says "Running independent copies side by side ... does not count." So no.

Kind: is it "copies" or "reframe"? The reframing changes the estimator slightly (pooling draws, rank-normalized R-hat), but the fundamental computation is the same MCMC, just many independent chains. It only runs the same computation more times, side by side. So "copies".

Proposal 3: Speculative multi-branch proposal evaluation. At each step evaluate k candidate proposals from the current state in parallel, combining via statistically valid multi-proposal Metropolis-Hastings. Does this remove a step-after-step dependency? The accept/reject decision at step t determines the starting point for step t+1. Evaluating k candidates in parallel within a step... Hmm. The multi-proposal MH kernel changes the computation: instead of one proposal per step, multiple proposals are considered and combined in a statistically valid update. This changes the kernel — it changes what is computed per step. Does it remove the dependency that one answer waits on? The chain steps still wait on previous decisions. The multi-proposal kernel computes multiple candidate evaluations at the same time — but these are candidates from the current state, which were previously done sequentially across steps (speculatively). Actually with branch-and-rollback prefetching, speculative evaluations reuse work that would otherwise be discarded. Hmm.

The question: does proposal 3 meet the criterion of removing a step-after-step dependency so that steps are computed at the same time? Speculative execution is a classic technique where future steps are computed before the current decision is made — i.e., the next proposal's likelihood is evaluated speculatively before knowing whether the current one is accepted. This does remove (or rather, bypasses) the waiting: the next step's evaluation is computed at the same time as the current one, with rollback if wrong. That is precisely "removes a step-after-step dependency that one answer waits on... so that those steps are computed at the same time."

Also the multi-proposal MH kernel: evaluating k candidates per step changes the kernel so that more compute per step buys more — that's a reframe (changes what is computed/ordered so more compute buys something it did not before). Yes, "reframe".

Meets criterion: yes — speculative/branch evaluation computes future-step proposals at the same time rather than waiting on the current decision. Actually, let me think more carefully. The multi-proposal MH: at each step, evaluate k candidate proposals from the current state in parallel. Previously, at each step only one proposal would be evaluated. Now k are evaluated simultaneously. The candidates all start from the current state, so they're not sequential steps being parallelized — they're alternatives within one step. But then "combine them via a statistically valid multi-proposal Metropolis-Hastings update" — this changes the kernel so that each transition uses more information, which can reduce the number of sequential steps needed. Hmm, does that "remove a step-after-step dependency that one answer waits on"? The chain still has sequential steps; each step still waits on the previous. But within a step, k proposals are computed at once instead of being computed across k sequential steps (each waiting on the prior decision). In a standard MH chain, evaluating k proposals would take k sequential steps, each waiting on the accept/reject decision of the previous. With multi-proposal MH, those k proposals are evaluated simultaneously, and the update combines them validly. So the step-after-step waiting is removed for those k proposals. I think this counts as "yes".

The criterion: "It removes a step-after-step dependency that one answer waits on (time steps, chain iterations or solver iterations), so that those steps are computed at the same time." For proposal 3, the next proposal evaluations no longer wait on the current decision — they're computed at the same time. Yes, meets criterion.

Kind: "reframe" — it changes what is computed (multi-proposal kernel instead of single-proposal) so more compute buys something it didn't before (higher ESS per step, fewer sequential steps).

Proposal 4: Neural likelihood emulator. This changes what is computed — instead of running the simulator, a surrogate is evaluated. This is a reframe? It changes what is computed (approximate likelihood instead of exact). More compute (offline) buys speed. Hmm. "reframe if it changes what is computed, measured or ordered so that more compute buys something it did not before" — the emulator replaces the sequential simulation with a batched surrogate evaluation. Does it remove a step-after-step dependency? The sequential daily recurrence inside each likelihood call is replaced by a surrogate mapping parameters to likelihood directly — so the time-step recurrence is no longer computed step-by-step; it's bypassed entirely. Hmm, is that "computed at the same time"? No — it's not that the time steps are computed simultaneously; it's that they're not computed at all, replaced by a learned function. That's more like a different algorithm, not a parallelization of the steps.

Actually, let's think about the kind classification. The emulator: changes what is computed (surrogate likelihood instead of exact). More compute (offline training runs, GPU batches) buys faster MCMC. That fits "reframe": it changes what is computed so that more compute buys something it did not before (offline compute buys faster inference). But wait — is the emulator itself a reframe of the parallelism problem? The criterion is about removing step-after-step dependencies. The emulator doesn't make the time steps computed at the same time; it eliminates them via approximation. The MCMC chain is still sequential. So meets_criterion: no.

Hmm, but is the emulator "reframe" or "other"? The definition: "reframe if it changes what is computed, measured or ordered so that more compute buys something it did not before". The emulator changes what is computed (approximate surrogate instead of exact simulation). Offline compute (10,000 simulator runs) buys online speed. So more compute buys something it did not before (fast approximate likelihoods). I'd classify as "reframe". Though one could argue it's "other" because it's an approximation, not a restructuring for parallelism. But per the given definition, it changes what is computed (surrogate vs exact) so that more (offline) compute buys speed — that fits "reframe". Hmm, but the spirit of "reframe" in these judgments is usually about reframing the sequential structure. Let me consider: the definitions given are the ones to apply strictly. "reframe: if it changes what is computed, measured or ordered so that more compute buys something it did not before". The emulator: what is computed changes (neural surrogate evaluations instead of simulator runs). More compute (offline runs, GPU training) buys faster calibration. Yes, that seems to fit "reframe".

Alternatively "other" because it doesn't restructure sequential dependencies; it just approximates. Hmm. The classification scheme: reframe / copies / other. "copies" = running same computation more times/on more items/side by side. "other" = otherwise. The emulator is not copies. Is it reframe? It changes what is computed — from exact likelihood to surrogate. And more compute (offline) buys something it did not before (fast approximate inference). I'll say "reframe", meets_criterion "no".

Actually wait. Let me reconsider. The "reframe" concept: "changes what is computed, measured or ordered so that more compute buys something it did not before". The emulator indeed changes what is computed during MCMC (surrogate instead of exact simulator). This is a change of what is computed, and more compute (offline training data) buys speed. So "reframe" seems right. But does it meet the specific criterion (removing step-after-step dependency so steps are computed at the same time)? No — the time steps are avoided/approximated, not computed simultaneously; the MCMC chain remains sequential. So meets_criterion: "no".

Proposal 5: Differentiable HMC. Replaces random-walk Metropolis (long sequential chains) with HMC/NUTS using gradients, taking fewer sequential steps to reach the same ESS. This changes what is computed (gradient-based trajectories instead of random walk) — more compute per step (leapfrog with gradients) buys fewer sequential steps. That's a "reframe": it changes what is computed/ordered so more compute buys something it did not before (fewer sequential steps for same ESS).

Does it meet the criterion? The criterion is about removing a step-after-step dependency so steps are computed at the same time. HMC doesn't compute chain steps simultaneously; it takes fewer, more informative steps. The chain is still sequential. Multiple leapfrog trajectories in parallel — that's independent trajectories side by side (copies-like) within warm-up? "run HMC or NUTS on GPU with multiple leapfrog trajectories in parallel" — parallel trajectories are side-by-side copies. The sequential dependency isn't removed; it's shortened. So meets_criterion: "no".

Hmm, but one could argue that HMC "removes a step-after-step dependency" in the sense that fewer sequential steps are needed... No — the criterion specifically says "so that those steps are computed at the same time". HMC doesn't compute the sequential steps at the same time; it reduces the number of steps. So "no".

Now, kind for proposal 5: "reframe" — changes what is computed (gradient-based trajectories) so more compute buys something it did not before (fewer sequential iterations). Yes, reframe.

Proposal 1 kind: "copies" — it keeps the recurrence exactly and vectorizes over parameter sets; same computation on more items side by side. Meets criterion: no — the time-step dependency remains; independent parameter sets run side by side.

Wait, but does proposal 1 change what is computed/ordered? "Keep the daily recurrence exactly but vectorize the state update over thousands of parameter sets" — this is running the same computation on more items (parameter sets) simultaneously. So "copies". Meets criterion: no — the per-step dependency within each parameter set remains; it's parallel copies across parameter sets, which doesn't count.

Proposal 2 kind: "copies" — hundreds of independent chains launched together = same computation (MCMC) run more times side by side. Meets criterion: no — independent chains side by side explicitly does not count.

Hmm, but proposal 2 also includes "rank-normalized early stopping" and pooling — but fundamentally it's many independent chains, i.e., copies. The criterion explicitly excludes running independent copies side by side. So no.

Proposal 3 kind: "reframe" — changes what is computed per step (k proposals combined via a valid multi-proposal MH update) so more compute buys more per step; also speculative evaluation computes next-step work before the decision. Meets criterion: yes — the next proposals no longer wait on the current accept/reject decision; they're evaluated at the same time and combined validly.

Let me double check proposal 3 against the criterion: "It removes a step-after-step dependency that one answer waits on (time steps, chain iterations or solver iterations), so that those steps are computed at the same time." Chain iterations: in standard MH, the next proposal's evaluation waits on the current accept/reject decision. With speculative/multi-branch evaluation, k candidate evaluations are computed at the same time, and the multi-proposal kernel combines them in a statistically valid way. So the waiting dependency is removed. Yes, meets criterion.

Actually, hold on. Is the multi-proposal evaluation truly removing the dependency, or just batching alternatives? The k candidates all start from the current state — so they're not sequential steps; they're parallel alternatives. But the sequential_part states: "The accept/reject decision at step t determines the starting point for step t+1, so the chain cannot evaluate the next proposal until the current decision is made." The restructure addresses exactly this: evaluate k candidate proposals from the current state in parallel (so they don't wait for each other), and combine via multi-proposal MH. In effect, what would have taken k sequential steps (each waiting on the prior decision) is now done in one parallel round with a valid combining rule. So yes, the step-after-step dependency is removed for those evaluations. meets_criterion: yes.

Proposal 4 kind: reframe or other? Let me think again. The emulator: "Build a GPU neural surrogate mapping parameters to likelihood values... evaluate the surrogate in large batches during MCMC, with periodic exact simulator re-evaluation." This changes what is computed (surrogate instead of exact simulator) — the sequential daily recurrence inside each likelihood call is replaced by a direct mapping. More compute (offline) buys something it did not before (fast approximate likelihood). So "reframe".

But one could argue "other": the emulator doesn't restructure the sequential dependency; it's a fundamentally different approach (approximation). Hmm. The kind definitions:
- reframe: changes what is computed, measured or ordered so that more compute buys something it did not before.
- copies: only runs the same computation more times, on more items, or side by side.
- other: otherwise.

The emulator changes what is computed (surrogate vs exact simulation). Offline compute buys online speed. That fits reframe. However, is the emulator a "reframing of the sequential problem"? The context: the research problem is about parallelization/reframing sequential dependencies. The reframing here is: instead of computing the sequential recurrence each time, learn it offline and evaluate in batches. The sequential time-stepping is distilled into weights. This changes what is computed so that more compute (offline) buys something (fast MCMC) it did not before. I'll classify as "reframe".

Meets criterion for 4: no — the time steps are not computed at the same time; they're replaced by a surrogate, and the MCMC chain remains sequential. The criterion requires steps to be computed at the same time; the emulator avoids computing them, and the chain iterations still wait on each other. So "no".

Hmm, wait. Could one argue that the emulator removes the sequential daily recurrence (a step-after-step dependency that one answer waits on)? The likelihood answer previously waited on the day-by-day recurrence. With the surrogate, the likelihood is computed directly without stepping. But the criterion says "so that those steps are computed at the same time" — the steps aren't computed at all; they're bypassed. So it doesn't meet the criterion as stated. "no".

Proposal 5 kind: reframe. "Rewrite the recurrence in a differentiable framework... run HMC or NUTS... taking fewer sequential steps to reach the same effective sample size." Changes what is computed (gradient-based trajectories) and the ordering (fewer sequential steps per unit ESS). More compute (gradients, parallel leapfrog) buys fewer sequential iterations. "reframe".

Meets criterion: no — chain transitions still wait on each other; parallel trajectories are side-by-side copies; the sequential dependency is reduced, not computed simultaneously.

Now let me also double-check proposal 1: could it be "reframe" because the ensemble likelihood evaluation is reframed so that the sequential time loop becomes "a short sequence of wide parallel kernels"? The restructure says "Keep the daily recurrence exactly but vectorize the state update over thousands of parameter sets... so the sequential time loop becomes a short sequence of wide parallel kernels." The time loop is still sequential (short sequence of steps); only the width across parameter sets is parallel. That's running the same computation on more items side by side — "copies". Meets criterion: no — time steps still depend on previous day; the parallelism is across independent parameter sets.

Proposal 2: "copies". The chains are independent copies. Also pooling draws — but that doesn't remove within-chain sequential dependency. no.

Now quotes. Pick a short quote from each proposal that supports the classification.

Proposal 1 quote: "Keep the daily recurrence exactly but vectorize the state update over thousands of parameter sets or catchments on a GPU" — this shows the recurrence (dependency) is kept, only parallelized across items. Reason: "Keeps day-to-day recurrence; parallelism is only across independent parameter sets, i.e., side-by-side copies." (under 25 words)

Proposal 2 quote: "Replace one long chain with hundreds of independent chains launched together on a GPU". Reason: independent chains run side by side; each chain remains sequential — explicitly excluded by criterion.

Proposal 3 quote: "At each step evaluate k candidate proposals from the current state in parallel on the GPU, then combine them via a statistically valid multi-proposal Metropolis-Hastings update". Reason: proposals that would otherwise wait on the accept/reject decision are evaluated simultaneously and combined validly; removes the step-after-step wait.

Proposal 4 quote: "Build a GPU neural surrogate mapping parameters to likelihood values or summary signatures from offline simulator runs". Reason: changes what is computed (approximate surrogate) but time steps are bypassed, not computed simultaneously; MCMC stays sequential.

Proposal 5 quote: "run HMC or NUTS on GPU with multiple leapfrog trajectories in parallel, taking fewer sequential steps to reach the same effective sample size". Reason: fewer sequential steps but steps still wait on each other; parallel trajectories are side-by-side copies.

Let me reconsider kind for 4 and 5 once more.

For 5: is it "reframe" or "other"? The reframe definition: "changes what is computed, measured or ordered so that more compute buys something it did not before". HMC changes what is computed per iteration (gradient-based leapfrog trajectories instead of random-walk proposals) and the ordering (fewer sequential steps for the same ESS). More compute (gradient evaluations) buys fewer sequential iterations — something it did not before. So "reframe". Yes.

For 4: The emulator changes what is computed (surrogate likelihood instead of exact simulation). More compute (offline training) buys fast inference. "reframe". Though some might say "other" because it's an approximation rather than a parallelization reframe. Hmm. Let me think about the intent. The three categories: reframe (changes what is computed/measured/ordered so more compute buys something new), copies (same computation more times/items/side by side), other. The emulator is definitely not copies. Is it reframe or other? The definition of reframe is broad: "changes what is computed... so that more compute buys something it did not before". The emulator changes what is computed during MCMC — instead of exact sequential simulations, batched surrogate evaluations. Offline compute buys something new: approximate-but-fast likelihoods. I think "reframe" is the intended classification. Alternatively, "other" if the scheme intends reframe to be specifically about restructuring sequential dependencies. But the given definition is broad and doesn't restrict to sequential dependencies — the criterion (meets_criterion) is the sequential-specific part. So kind: reframe for 4.

Hmm, actually, let me reconsider. Maybe the scheme is: "reframe" = changes what is computed/measured/ordered so more compute buys something (this is the general category of good reframings); "copies" = trivial parallelism; "other" = neither (e.g., approximations that don't involve compute trade-offs, or things that don't parallelize). The emulator: more compute (offline simulation runs, training) buys faster MCMC. That's compute buying something new. So reframe.

But wait — the emulator also doesn't really reframe the sequential structure; it sidesteps it with approximation. Yet per the literal definition, "changes what is computed" — yes, surrogate instead of simulator. "so that more compute buys something it did not before" — yes, offline compute buys online speed. I'll go with "reframe".

Alternatively, some might argue the emulator is "other" because it changes the computation itself (different algorithm) rather than reframing for parallelism. But the definition says "changes what is computed... so that more compute buys something it did not before" — the emulator fits this. And "other" would be for things that neither reframe nor copy. The emulator clearly changes what is computed and leverages more compute (offline) — reframe.

Hmm, but actually there's a subtlety: is the emulator's speedup from "more compute"? Yes — 10,000 offline simulator runs + training compute buys fast surrogate evaluations. So more compute buys something (fast approximate inference) it did not before. reframe.

Meets criterion for 4: no. The sequential daily recurrence and the MCMC chain's sequential dependencies are avoided, not computed simultaneously. The criterion says steps must be "computed at the same time". Bypassing ≠ computing simultaneously. "no".

Let me now also reconsider proposal 3's meets_criterion more carefully. The criterion: "It removes a step-after-step dependency that one answer waits on (time steps, chain iterations or solver iterations), so that those steps are computed at the same time. Running independent copies side by side, or splitting each single step across GPUs, does not count."

Proposal 3's sequential_part: "The accept/reject decision at step t determines the starting point for step t+1, so the chain cannot evaluate the next proposal until the current decision is made." The restructure: "At each step evaluate k candidate proposals from the current state in parallel on the GPU, then combine them via a statistically valid multi-proposal Metropolis-Hastings update, or use branch-and-rollback prefetching to reuse speculative evaluations."

Does this remove the step-after-step dependency? In the multi-proposal kernel, yes: the k proposals don't wait for each other's acceptance decisions; they're evaluated simultaneously and combined via a valid update. The chain iterations that would each wait on a decision are now computed at the same time (as parallel candidate branches) and merged. This is exactly the speculative-execution pattern the criterion describes: steps that one answer waits on are computed at the same time. Also branch-and-rollback prefetching explicitly computes future-step evaluations before the decision — speculative computation. So "yes".

Is it "independent copies side by side"? The k candidates are alternatives, not independent chains — they get combined into one chain state via the multi-proposal update. So it's not just copies; it's a valid parallelized transition. Yes, meets criterion.

One might argue: the k candidates all start from the same current state, so they're "independent copies" of proposal evaluation... but they're not copies of the same computation — they're different proposals (k candidate proposals), and crucially they're combined via a statistically valid update, meaning the chain's sequential processing of proposals is genuinely parallelized. In standard MH, processing k proposals takes k sequential iterations each waiting on the previous decision; here they're done at once. That's removing the step-after-step dependency. yes.

Now the quotes — need to be from the proposal text. Let me pick:

1: quote: "Keep the daily recurrence exactly but vectorize the state update over thousands of parameter sets or catchments on a GPU" — reason: "Daily time-step dependency is kept; parallelism only runs independent parameter sets side by side." (13 words)

2: quote: "Replace one long chain with hundreds of independent chains launched together on a GPU" — reason: "Independent chains are copies run side by side; each chain's iterations still wait sequentially." (14 words)

3: quote: "At each step evaluate k candidate proposals from the current state in parallel on the GPU, then combine them via a statistically valid multi-proposal Metropolis-Hastings update" — reason: "Proposals no longer wait on the accept/reject decision; they're evaluated simultaneously and validly combined." (~14 words)

4: quote: "Build a GPU neural surrogate mapping parameters to likelihood values or summary signatures from offline simulator runs" — reason: "Changes what is computed (approximate surrogate), but sequential steps are bypassed, not computed simultaneously." (~14 words)

5: quote: "run HMC or NUTS on GPU with multiple leapfrog trajectories in parallel, taking fewer sequential steps to reach the same effective sample size" — reason: "Fewer sequential steps, but chain transitions still wait on each other; parallel trajectories are side-by-side copies." (~16 words)

Reasons at most 25 words each. Good.

Let me double check word counts:

1: "Daily time-step dependency is kept; parallelism only runs independent parameter sets side by side." = 14 words. Good.
2: "Independent chains are copies run side by side; each chain's iterations still wait sequentially." = 14 words. Good.
3: "Proposals no longer wait on the current accept/reject decision; they are evaluated simultaneously and combined validly." = 16 words. Good.
4: "Changes what is computed (approximate surrogate), but sequential steps are bypassed, not computed simultaneously; MCMC stays sequential." = 17 words. Good.
5: "Fewer sequential steps, but chain transitions still wait on each other; parallel trajectories are side-by-side copies." = 16 words. Good.
